topic: The plague with and without the article
claim: Some common infectious diseases optionally take the definite article ((the) flu, (the) measles). With the plague, the article is obligatory.
evidence_summary: OED plague, n. sense 3c, the disease caused by Yersinia pestis: “Frequently in the plague.” Bare plague occurs in its quotations, e.g. during the prevalence of plague (E. W. Lane, 1841). The WHO fact sheet has Plague is an infectious disease and effective against plague. In the have frame, the OED’s one example keeps the article: suspected of having the plague (Times, 1994).
finding: The article is frequent, not obligatory, with this noun. The claim may hold for the have frame of [17iii], which none of the sources tests with a bare noun.
proposed_wording: With plague, the article is usual, especially after have: He has the plague.
inference: Does the disease noun plague require the definite article?

evidence.example: Sense 3c: “Frequently in the plague.” 1841 Some Muslims even shut themselves up during the prevalence of plague (Lane). 1994 eight people suspected of having the plague (Times).
evidence.establishes: An edited dictionary treats the article as frequent rather than required. The have-frame example has the article.
evidence.locator: Meaning & use, sense 3c. Accessed 19 November 2026 through the University of Toronto Libraries subscription.

evidence.source: World Health Organization, Plague fact sheet.
evidence.example: “Plague is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis”; “Antibiotics and supportive therapy are effective against plague”.
evidence.establishes: Current edited medical prose uses bare plague as subject and as object of a preposition.
evidence.locator: Key facts and treatment sections. Fetched by a reader on 19 November 2026.
